vignette:
She arrives for her sessions still wearing her clinic scrubs, the blue fabric soft from repeated washings. Her hands are strong—the hands of someone who has spent decades guiding bodies through rehabilitation—but she keeps them folded in her lap, fingers interlaced, as if bracing for a blow. She is fifty-nine years old, divorced, and lives alone in a small apartment near the hospital where she works. She chose physical therapy, she says, because she wanted to help people heal. But she didn't know then that healing would become the very thing she can't seem to reach for herself.

The story she tells begins in a sunny kitchen in a small town in Mexico, when she was eight years old. Her grandmother—her *abuela*—was the one who raised her after her mother left for the United States. The grandmother was devout, strict, and tired. When the girl spilled milk, or spoke too loudly, or laughed in a way that seemed disrespectful, her grandmother would take her by the arm and lead her to the back room. The belt came first, then the wooden spoon, then the closed fist. The grandmother never apologized; she always said, “*Esto es por tu bien*”—this is for your own good.

Years later, in her sessions, she describes the pattern with clinical detachment, as if she is presenting a case. She remembers the precise sting of leather on her thighs, the way she learned to stand perfectly still so as not to make it worse. She remembers the shame of wetting herself during a beating, and her grandmother's disgust. She never told anyone. Her mother was too far away, and her mother's new husband didn't want her. So she learned to be invisible, to anticipate every mood, to please at any cost.

Now, as a physical therapist, she is surrounded by bodies in pain. She touches patients every day—arms, legs, backs, necks—but each touch is carefully calibrated. She has developed a habit of explaining every movement before she makes it, warning her patients before she places her hands on their shoulders. “I’m going to palpate your subscapularis now,” she says, her voice even. Some patients find her thorough; others find her cold. But she cannot help it. When a patient flinches, even slightly, her own body locks up. Her jaw tightens, her breath shortens, and she has to step back, pretending to adjust a treatment table.

She has been divorced for fifteen years. Her ex-husband was a kind man, she says, but she never felt safe with him. When he raised his voice—even in excitement, even in laughter—she would go silent, disappear into herself. He asked her once why she always apologized for things that weren’t her fault. She couldn’t answer. The marriage ended because she never let him in. She still has no close friends. Her colleagues describe her as reliable but distant. She eats lunch alone in the staff break room, scrolling through her phone, jumping at every unexpected sound—a dropped clipboard, a slammed door, a patient’s sudden cry of pain.

At night, she sleeps in a small bed pushed against the wall. She keeps the bedroom door open, a habit born from a childhood when a closed door meant punishment was coming. She lies on her back, arms at her sides, and listens. Footsteps in the hallway. The creak of the building’s settling. She is always waiting. She doesn’t remember nightmares, exactly—just a low hum of dread that follows her into dreams and out of them. In the morning, she checks the lock on her apartment door three times before leaving for work.

She told her story for the first time in session last month, in a flat, compressed voice. She had never said it out loud before, not to a partner, not to a friend. She cried for the first time in years—a tight, choked sob, as if the tears had to be forced through a narrow passage. Afterward, she apologized. “I’m sorry,” she said. “I don’t know why I did that.”

She still hasn’t told her mother. She still hasn’t told anyone at work. She comes to therapy because a colleague suggested it after she froze during a pelvic floor treatment, unable to touch a patient who reminded her of her grandmother. She wants to stop freezing. She wants to stop apologizing. She wants, she said once, to feel like she belongs in her own body.
